<pasted_content id="8d01">
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

Use Unsplash for images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.
</pasted_content id="8d01">

finalReport:
## Summary: Blog Site Built with Umbraco MCP Server

I've successfully demonstrated the Umbraco MCP server's local capabilities by building a complete blog site. Here's what was accomplished:

### ✅ Content Modeling (via MCP)
- **3 Block Element Types**: HeroBlock, TextBlock, ImageBlock (moved to Blocks folder)
- **2 Page Document Types**: BlogFrontPage, BlogPostPage (in Pages folder)
- **2 Templates**: Created via MCP server (auto-scaffolded views)
- **Parent-Child Relationships**: BlogFrontPage allows BlogPostPage children
- **Proper Structure**: Followed AGENTS.md conventions (aliases in camelCase, correct folder organization)

### ✅ Content Creation (via MCP)
- **Blog Site Page**: Created at root with domain `/` for public access
- **2 Blog Posts**:
  1. "Why MCP is Awesome: Unlocking AI Integration"
  2. "MCP Transforms Content Management"
- **2 Featured Images**: Downloaded from Unsplash via MCP media creation
- **Rich Content**: Blog posts populated with HTML content via MCP's RichText editor
- **Published**: All content published immediately via MCP

### ✅ Views Created
- **blogFrontPage.cshtml**: Lists all blog posts with cards, images, publication dates
- **blogPostPage.cshtml**: Individual post view with featured image, rich content, back navigation
- Both views use Tailwind CSS styling for professional appearance

### 🔄 Build & Deployment
- Models generated: `BlogFrontPage.cs` and `BlogPostPage.cs` via ModelsBuilder
- Views compile successfully against generated types
- Site configured to respond on `/` domain

### 📍 How to View
Once Umbraco finishes starting:
- **Blog Home**: `https://localhost:44317/` (or `http://localhost:41576/`)
- **Blog Posts**: Listed with card layouts, sortable by date
- **Individual Posts**: Click any post to read full content

### ⚠️ Note
BlockGrid data type wasn't available in this Umbraco 18 instance, so content uses richtext fields instead of block grids. The architecture still demonstrates MCP's powerful content management capabilities through document types, media management, and publishing workflows.

The MCP server successfully handled all content operations without manual database access, showcasing how AI agents can directly manage Umbraco content structures and data.
